cards.headline: Pro-government forces in Yemen withdraw from Bab al-Mandab area

pages.text: Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia are withdrawing from an area overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, leaving the strategic waterway under the control of the Iran-backed Houthi movement. On November 15, 2026, the Southern Armed Forces stated they were withdrawing troops from the Bab al-Mandab area and Dhubab Airport to reinforce other front lines and address existing threats, identifying the southern city of Aden as a priority for defense. Houthi-run media reported later on November 15, 2026, that the group had taken control of the territory. This shift ends a weeks-long offensive by pro-government forces to secure the area near the shipping gateway following a surprise Houthi offensive in September that squeezed global oil exports and caused thousands to flee.

The Bab al-Mandab Strait is a vital global shipping route at the southern end of the Red Sea. The Houthi seizure of territory near the waterway, including the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island at the mouth of the strait, contributed to a surge in global oil prices. This occurred because Saudi Arabia has been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the war between the US, Israel, and Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz. While the Houthis stated they posed no threat to international shipping when they captured the area, they said they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia. In response to Houthi actions, Saudi Arabia has conducted hundreds of air strikes, while the Houthis have launched hundreds of drones and missiles at Saudi cities and infrastructure.

The Muslim World League (MWL) condemned repeated Houthi attacks using ballistic missiles and drones targeting civilian areas and the Makkah region in Saudi Arabia. MWL Secretary-General Mohammed Al-Issa stated the group is employing a “terrorist approach characteristic of militias” that violates Muslim sanctities and endangers lives. According to the Saudi Press Agency, Al-Issa reaffirmed the MWL's support for measures taken by Saudi authorities to protect Muslim sites. Separately, Turki Al-Maliki, spokesperson for the Coalition to Support Legitimacy in Yemen, said Saudi air defense intercepted and destroyed two drones in the Madinah region, while other reports indicated two drones were intercepted and destroyed in the Makkah region.

cards.headline: Iran launches drone attacks against US military base in Bahrain

pages.text: Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) launched six drones targeting a US air defence radar at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base in Bahrain. The IRGC described the attack as a response to “hostile US actions” and “blatant aggression of the U.S. military.” This marks the second Iranian drone attack in three days and the first direct strike on Bahrain in weeks. Bahraini authorities stated that air defences intercepted the drones and destroyed the projectiles before they reached their targets, though the IRGC reported a “successful impact.”

The strikes follow a series of US military strikes against Iranian targets in recent weeks, including Qeshm Island in the strait of Hormuz. US President Donald Trump characterized these as minor strikes and noted that Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states had cautioned him against large-scale combat operations. Trump also stated that Washington is no longer seeking a deal with Iran and said he instructed Vice-President JD Vance to shift his focus to alleged corruption and fraud in Democrat-run cities and states. However, Reuters reported that Trump said over the weekend he was considering holding off on attacking Iran absent new provocations.

In Tehran, foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said Iran would continue to respond to military aggression by the US or other states, adding that Iran is focused on its security and is “not waiting for anyone.” Regional tensions have been further complicated by other developments: Iran claimed a mine sank an oil supertanker in the strait of Hormuz, and in Yemen, Iran’s Houthi allies advanced against pro-government forces in the south, potentially opening a route to Aden.

cards.headline: Yemen’s southern forces redeploy troops to bolster Aden's defenses

pages.text: Yemen’s Southern Armed Forces are redeploying troops from Dhubab Airport and the Bab Al-Mandab area in western Taiz province to reinforce the capital, Aden, and neighboring provinces. The Southern Armed Forces stated the move is part of a broader reorganization to address security threats and reinforce front lines. This redeployment follows reports on November 15, 2026, that Houthi forces were advancing toward Aden, positioned approximately 60 kilometers from the city at the al-Kharaz camp in al-Madariba. Sources within government forces and the government reported that the Houthis had seized control of two districts in Lahj province during this advance.

Majed Al-Nuzaili, a military spokesman for the Yemeni government, welcomed the redeployment, stating that defending Aden and lifting the Houthi siege of Taiz are linked national responsibilities. Al-Nuzaili noted that the move builds on efforts by the Popular Resistance and southern forces. He also called for international and regional coordination to secure the Bab Al-Mandab Strait, citing its importance to global trade and shipping. Operations to lift the siege of Taiz are expected to continue with support from the Coalition to Restore Legitimacy in Yemen. In a separate statement, Al-Nuzaili reported that Yemen’s armed forces carried out 906 strikes against Houthi targets across several fronts. These strikes included 41 airstrikes, 18 drone strikes, 90 rocket launcher strikes, and 757 artillery strikes. Al-Nuzaili stated these attacks targeted Houthi fortifications, troop concentrations, positions, and military equipment, resulting in the neutralization of 201 fighters and field commanders and the destruction or disabling of 121 pieces of equipment and military vehicles.

cards.headline: Iran says supertanker with more than 2 million barrels of oil sank in the Gulf

pages.text: The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps stated that a supertanker carrying more than two million barrels of crude oil sank in the southern waters of the Persian Gulf after striking a naval mine and catching fire. The Guard Corps, according to a statement carried by state TV, said two oil tankers traveling along an unauthorized route in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz struck naval mines, resulting in massive explosions and fire. The statement did not specify the names or origins of the tankers, and there has been no independent confirmation of these incidents. A British maritime monitor noted it was aware of a report from Indian shipping authorities regarding an attack on a tanker in the Gulf, but it was unclear if this was the same incident announced by the Iranian Guards.

The Strait of Hormuz is a vital trade corridor that normally carries approximately one-fifth of global oil. Since the outbreak of the Middle East war in late February, Tehran has heavily restricted traffic through the waterway, insisting vessels use routes authorized by Iran and regularly targeting ships that transit without such authorization. In response, the United States has imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports and has helped tankers travel the strait. US Central Command, which oversees US military operations in the region, said it has helped Gulf countries export 1.5 billion barrels of oil via Hormuz since the summer. The American military recently claimed to have cleared all mines from the main routes through the waterway.

cards.headline: Haitians welcome deployment of approximately 2,000 Salvadoran troops to combat gang violence

pages.text: Haitians have welcomed the deployment of approximately 2,000 Salvadoran soldiers to Port-au-Prince to assist in fighting gang violence. The troops are currently guarding the capital's main stadium, which Haitian security forces regained control of on November 12, 2026, after it had been under gang control for two years. El Salvador President Nayib Bukele stated the stadium will serve as an operational base for the troops. Bukele, an authoritarian leader who gained attention for suppressing gangs in El Salvador but has faced accusations of human rights violations, said his soldiers will launch an offensive from the stadium. In a post on X written in Haitian Creole, Bukele urged gang members to abandon the area, stating that those who choose to stay and fight will face consequences.

The deployment was first ordered by President Bukele to rescue four Salvadoran soldiers who went missing following an ambush in Port-au-Prince. Gang control over large areas of the city expanded following the 2021 assassination of President Jovenel Moïse. Experts suggest many Haitians welcome a hardline crackdown similar to Bukele's approach in El Salvador because extreme conditions have left many desperate for relief from gang rule. One displaced man expressed feeling pride at the prospect of regaining freedom following the arrival of Bukele's forces. Port-au-Prince resident Venet Demogene noted that Haitians have no other country to go to and expressed a desire to live in their own home.

cards.headline: Runoff election scheduled for November 29 in pro-Russian Gagauzia region of Moldova

pages.text: Gagauzia, an autonomous, pro-Russian territory in southern Moldova, will hold a runoff election on November 29 to select a new leader. The runoff follows a November 16 election in which no candidate secured a majority of the vote. According to Reuters, former Moldovan presidential candidate Alexandr Stoianoglo, who secured 38.44% of the vote, will face Fiodor Gagauz, a representative of the pro-Russian Socialist Party who received 24.22% of the vote, in the upcoming vote. This election aims to replace the region's former leader, known as a bashkan, who was recently jailed. The regional vote occurs as Moldova seeks to join the European Union and faces tensions with Russia regarding frequent drone incursions.

The election follows the arrest and sentencing of Gagauzia's former bashkan, Evghenia Gutul. In August 2025, Gutul was sentenced to seven years in prison for systematically bringing funds from Russia to Moldova to support the pro-Russian Shor Party. Prosecutors stated that between 2019 and 2022, Gutul received a total of 42.5 million Moldovan lei (approximately $2.5 million) used by the Shor Party to pay for anti-government protests and other purposes. Gagauzia is an autonomous territory that partly borders Ukraine's Odesa Oblast and has traditionally favored closer relations with Russia while opposing EU integration.

cards.headline: Cape Verde President Jose Maria Neves set to win second term according to provisional results

pages.text: President Jose Maria Neves is favored to win re-election in Cape Verde, with provisional results from the country's electoral commission showing he secured 63.8% of the vote. The 66-year-old Neves, who is backed by the African Party for the Independence of Cape Verde (PAICV), is seeking a second term as leader of the West African archipelago. His main challenger, 61-year-old former justice minister Joana Rosa Amado, secured approximately 31.6% of the vote. Four other candidates also contested the election, which was monitored by about 150 observers from the African Union, the European Union, and the Economic Community of West African States. Approximately 420,000 people were eligible to vote in the nation.

Cape Verde is an archipelago of ten volcanic islands located in the Atlantic Ocean, about 600 kilometers off the coast of Senegal. The nation is recognized for its democratic stability and good governance; the Mo Ibrahim Foundation's 2026 index on global governance ranks the country third among Africa's 54 nations, following only Seychelles and Mauritius. The World Bank classifies Cape Verde as an upper-middle-income country, a status supported by a growing tourism industry and a 16.8% increase in gross national income per capita between 2023 and 2024. Despite this growth, the country faces challenges including social inequality, geographic isolation, a lack of travel options between islands, rising energy prices, an increased cost of living, and youth unemployment.

cards.headline: Syrian Electricity Co. signs deal with Czech firm to rehabilitate Aleppo power plant units

pages.text: The Syrian Electricity Co. has signed an agreement with the Czech firm Energy Care to rehabilitate three generating units at the Aleppo Thermal Power Plant. Once completed, the project is expected to restore a combined 639 megawatts of generating capacity. The Aleppo plant is one of Syria's largest power stations and serves as a major electricity source for northern Syria. This agreement is part of the Energy Ministry's efforts to restore generating capacity and improve the reliability of the national electricity grid through the rehabilitation of power stations. The deal was signed at the Energy Ministry’s headquarters in Damascus in the presence of Energy Minister Mohammad Al-Bashir and the Czech Ambassador to the Syrian Arab Republic, Vitezslav Pivonka. Imad Abu Ali, the director of the plant, signed for the Syrian company, while Haitham Eid, Energy Care’s representative in Syria, signed for the Czech firm.

The agreement covers the rehabilitation of the plant’s second, third, and fourth generating units, which each have a design capacity of 213 MW. According to the project timetable, the third unit is scheduled to return to service 18 months after work begins, the fourth unit after 24 months, and the second unit after 30 months. Once all three units are operational, the plant’s total design generating capacity is expected to be approximately 1,040 MW, which includes about 400 MW from the first and fifth units. This follows previous maintenance work at the plant to address technical faults in main and auxiliary systems, such as water treatment equipment, forced-draft air systems, and rotary air preheaters. In May, Abu Ali stated that repairs to the first and fifth units had increased electricity output to 195 MW from the first unit and 202 MW from the fifth unit.

cards.headline: Bangladesh apparel exports to EU fell 11.91% to €13.48 billion

pages.text: Bangladesh’s apparel exports to the European Union (EU) fell 11.91 percent to €13.48 billion during the January-September period, according to Eurostat data. This decline represented the steepest drop among the EU’s 11 largest suppliers during that timeframe. Bangladesh lost €1.82 billion in export value, an amount exceeding the €1.78 billion lost by the entire EU market. Consequently, Bangladesh’s share of EU imports decreased from 21.10 percent to 19.06 percent.

The decline in export value was driven in part by falling prices, which accounted for slightly more than half of the lost value. During the January-September period, the export volume fell 5.74 percent and the unit price fell 6.54 percent to €13.70 per kg, a rate approximately 30 percent below the EU average. The downward trend occurred in stages: exports were down 20.89 percent in January-April, remained nearly level at a 1.25 percent decrease in May-August, and fell by 9.49 percent in September alone.

Among major suppliers, China was the only one to grow in both value and volume, with exports rising 4.46 percent to €24.25 billion and its share increasing from 32.02 percent to 34.29 percent. Vietnam’s export value rose 4.33 percent to €3.47 billion despite a 3.55 percent fall in volume, as its unit price rose 8.18 percent. Other suppliers showed mixed results: Cambodia raised its unit price by 8.42 percent, while Pakistan increased volume by 1.22 percent but cut its unit price by 11.37 percent to €10.90 per kg, the lowest among major suppliers.

cards.headline: More than 158,000 signatories, including Elon Musk, call for Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang

pages.text: Elon Musk, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Y Combinator president Garry Tan are among more than 158,000 people signing an open letter calling for Nvidia's board to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive. The letter, which includes more than 7,500 Nvidia employees, demands that the board “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts.” This campaign follows Huang's resignation on November 12, 2026, from the AI chip company he co-founded and led for 33 years. An ally of Huang told the Financial Times that a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives is being formed to lobby for his return and seek support from the White House. Huang has reportedly discussed a possible return to the company with people close to him.

Huang resigned following reports that he engaged in at least two extramarital affairs, one involving a subordinate and another with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman. Reuters reported that Huang allegedly misled senior Nvidia executives, including general counsel Tim Teter and chief marketing officer Alison Wagonfeld, regarding the nature of his relationship with Alice Huang. According to Reuters, Huang described his interactions with Alice Huang and her company, Megaspeed International, as ordinary customer-related business dealings in messages sent during 2025 and October 2026, but two people familiar with the matter told Reuters he did not disclose the relationship was romantic. Alice Huang has been the subject of US scrutiny over alleged ties to Chinese intelligence activities.

The push for Huang's return faces opposition from US officials and lawmakers. On November 15, 2026, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News that Nvidia should look “outside” the company for its next chief and called for a “dramatic shake-up.” Bessent also questioned whether Nvidia knowingly allowed its most advanced AI chips to reach China, noting this was more important than the affair. The US forbids sales to China of the most cutting-edge AI chips to maintain a lead in the artificial intelligence race. Meanwhile, US lawmakers from both sides of the aisle have demanded Huang and Nvidia appear before Congress to investigate whether US national security was put at risk. On November 13, 2026, investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker urged the Nvidia board to keep “all options” open.

cards.headline: Estonia to close all border crossings with Russia following attempted attack on drone manufacturer

pages.text: Estonia will close all its border crossings with Russia starting 1 December following a suspected sabotage attack on a defense company in Viimsi. Authorities stated the attack was ordered by Russia’s GRU military intelligence service. The planned closure affects three crossings: Narva in the north, and Koidula and Luhamaa in the south. Authorities have not specified how long the border will remain closed. Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said the decision aims to reduce Russia's ability to conduct hostile activities in Estonia and strengthen efforts to prevent sanctions circumvention. Tsahkna noted he informed his counterparts in Finland, Latvia, and Lithuania of the decision.

On the morning of November 14, 2026, eight people were detained during an attempted attack on Threod Systems, a defense company that manufactures long-range attack and reconnaissance drones. Estonia’s internal security service, Kapo, said the attack was intended to cause an explosion and set the building on fire. While one report indicated no injuries or damage occurred after the company’s security team responded, Prime Minister Kristen Michal stated that law enforcement prevented extensive damage. Authorities have requested a court order for five of the detained individuals to remain in custody, according to Estonia’s public broadcaster ERR.

Prime Minister Kristen Michal linked the attack to Estonia’s ongoing support for Ukraine, describing it as part of a broader hybrid war—a strategy involving non-military methods like sabotage to achieve political goals—aimed at making Estonia hesitate and weakening support for Ukraine. Michal stated the border closure is necessary to reduce the risk of further attacks and to signal that attacks on Estonia’s defense industry are unacceptable. Foreign Minister Tsahkna added that Russia must understand that attempts to intimidate or destabilize Estonian security will face consequences.

cards.headline: International Court of Justice to rule on whether Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya

pages.text: The International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague will deliver a judgment on the morning of November 19, 2026, regarding whether Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority. This case follows a military campaign nearly a decade ago that forced hundreds of thousands of Muslim Rohingya to flee across the border. The ruling is expected to set a 21st-century benchmark for international law, as the ICJ has never before found a state responsible for genocide, a crime defined after the Nazi-led Holocaust as acts committed with the intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial, or religious group. The decision will also have implications for a separate high-profile genocide case against Israel.

The ICJ judges have spent seven years weighing accusations brought by The Gambia, a Muslim-majority state, alleging that Myanmar’s repression of the Rohingya breached the 1948 UN genocide convention. A central legal challenge in such cases is proving “intent,” which is required to meet the definition of genocide. Antonia Mulvey, founder of Legal Action Worldwide (Law)—an organization representing hundreds of Rohingya survivors—said she is “cautiously optimistic” the court will hold Myanmar fully accountable. Mulvey stated that government actions showed “patterns of conduct” proving clear attempts to destroy the group, noting that attacks on villages occurred in the same manner.

Yanghee Lee, a former UN rights investigator to Myanmar, described the upcoming ruling as “historic for Rohingya survivors and their families around the world.” Lee noted that the international community failed to prevent Myanmar military atrocities against the Rohingya nine years ago and stated that the court must seize this opportunity to secure justice and reckon with those failings.

cards.headline: Germany's 2027 draft budget proposes €561 billion in spending amid €123 billion shortfall

pages.text: Germany's Budget Committee concluded a final session at 5:55 a.m. on November 13, 2026, following nearly 16 hours of negotiations to finalize a draft for the 2027 federal budget. The proposal outlines approximately €561 billion ($620 billion) in planned spending, but the federal government expects a revenue shortfall of €123 billion, which will require borrowing to bridge the gap. This new debt would be added to existing loans used for defense spending and the renovation of infrastructure. The draft budget is now set for a final vote in the Bundestag on November 27.

The draft budget received votes in favor from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) and its coalition partners, the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU). cards.headline: Estimated 350,000 people rally in Prague against plan to fund broadcasters from state budget

pages.text: An estimated 350,000 people gathered at Letná Plain in Prague to protest a government plan to scrap mandatory licence fees for Czechia’s public broadcasters. Organisers said the demonstration, which aimed to save the fees that currently fund the broadcasters, was one of the largest in the country’s history. The Million Moments for Democracy group, which organised the event, issued a statement demanding the government withdraw the plan and expressing concern that Prime Minister Andrej Babiš and his coalition partners pose a threat to democracy. The coalition includes populist, hard-right nationalist, and Eurosceptic parties. Many protesters wore triangular paper hats modeled after Večerníček, a children’s bedtime story mascot that has become a symbol of the protest, while others carried banners stating, “We won’t give media away.”

The proposed legislation would replace mandatory licence fees with funding provided directly from the state budget. Protesters argue this shift would grant government ministers more leverage over newsrooms, potentially eroding media independence. Demonstrators compared the move to actions in Hungary, Poland, Serbia, and Slovakia, where current or previous right-wing populist governments have reduced media autonomy. The current wave of unrest follows a series of protests held since late October, after the first reading of the bill to scrap the licence fees was pushed through during the night. These demonstrations follow weeks of protests in various towns and cities, as well as a strike by staff at Czech Radio and Czech TV.

cards.headline: Alberta government asks judge to dismiss First Nation's challenge of sovereignty act

pages.text: The Alberta government is asking a judge to strike down a constitutional challenge brought by the Onion Lake Cree Nation regarding the Alberta Sovereignty within a United Canada Act. Lawyers argued in an Edmonton court for the government's application to stop the claim from proceeding to trial, with the province arguing that the First Nation has not shown the act has had any impact on treaty rights. Court of King's Bench Justice Grant Dunlop has reserved his decision on the matter. The Onion Lake Cree Nation, which straddles the Alberta-Saskatchewan boundary, argues the act is unconstitutional because it conflicts with the Treaty 6 relationship with the Crown and has asked the court to declare the law unenforceable. Chief Pete Chief told reporters outside the court that the law was passed without meaningful consultation and raises questions about treaty rights and the limits of provincial authority, stating that treaty rights existed before Alberta was created and did not disappear when the province was established.

The Alberta Sovereignty within a United Canada Act was the flagship first law of Premier Danielle Smith, who used it as a signature proposal during her 2022 leadership win of the United Conservative Party. Smith stated the act was necessary to resist federal encroachment into provincial jurisdiction. When Smith first invoked the law, she conceded that it was symbolic and that she did not need it to implement new measures to oppose federal energy regulations. The province maintains that the act does not authorize anything that would contravene federal law or the Canadian Constitution.

cards.headline: Bank of England chief economist signals likely interest rate rises to combat inflation

pages.text: Bank of England chief economist Huw Pill has stated that the central bank will probably need to raise interest rates again, potentially in early 2027, to combat rising inflation. This follows a recent decision to increase interest rates from 3.75% to 4%. Pill told the Financial Times that while the recent increase was a “significant step” toward improving monetary policy, “we have further to go.” The move signals a potential rise in mortgage payments for an estimated 2.3 million homeowners who must refinance their loans. Pill indicated he is poised to vote for another quarter-point increase, noting his view that the central bank “waited too long” to act against inflation.

Inflation is expected to rise to 5% in spring, driven by high oil and gas prices resulting from the Iran war. Pill expects public and private sector workers to demand substantial pay rises, which he believes could keep inflation high for a longer period. He expressed concern that the inflationary impact could be magnified by “second-round effects,” where wage increases lead to further price hikes. Pill told the Financial Times that he considers an end to the US-Israeli conflict with Iran and a fall in energy prices to be a “very low probability.” While the Bank has not yet seen evidence of companies passing higher costs to consumers or significant wage increases, Pill stated that “the absence of evidence was not evidence of absence.” Financial markets expect UK interest rates to rise to almost 5% in 2027.

cards.headline: Investigators in Hungary find $19.5m in hidden cash during corruption probe

pages.text: Hungarian investigators seized $19.5m in cash, including bundles buried in forests, during searches conducted on November 12 and 13, 2026. The National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH), a new agency established to investigate the suspected misuse of public money, reported that the money was found in Budapest and three other parts of Hungary. This discovery is part of an investigation into Miklos Sesztak, who served as Hungary’s development minister from 2014 to 2018. cards.headline: Turkey's approval of Makkah Defence Pact takes effect following separate agreement with Qatar

pages.text: Turkey's law approving the Makkah Defence Pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan has taken effect following its publication in the country's official gazette. This legislative step follows the Turkish parliament's ratification of the agreement on November 5, which passed with 279 votes to 119. The Makkah Defence Pact, signed by Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan in August, is modeled after NATO's Article 5, meaning an attack on one member is considered an attack on all. The pact aims to strengthen intelligence sharing, military co-ordination, and defence industry co-operation among the three nations. cards.headline: New U.S. national policy for organ retrieval procedure sparks ethical debate

pages.text: The U.S. organ transplant system has approved the first national policy for a controversial procedure used to remove organs from hospital patients. The procedure, called normothermic regional perfusion (NRP), involves doctors attaching an external pump to a donor minutes after their circulation has ended and they have been declared dead. This pump restores blood flow to the donor's heart, lungs, kidneys, liver, and other organs to prevent them from deteriorating. Dr. Raymond Lynch, the director of transplantation at the Health Resources & Services Administration—the federal agency that oversees the organ transplant system—stated that the hope for NRP is that it increases both the supply and the quality of organs, which could help solve the chronic organ shortage.

The procedure can be used after a family has decided to withdraw care because there is no hope of meaningful recovery for the person. cards.headline: US officials and experts call for crackdown on illegal mining as 60% of Ghana's freshwater sources face degradation

pages.text: United States officials and scientific experts are calling for an urgent crackdown on galamsey—illegal small-scale gold mining—to address mercury pollution that has degraded an estimated 60 per cent of Ghana’s freshwater sources. During a symposium in Accra on November 10, 2026, experts warned that the pollution threatens public health, food security, and economic opportunity by contaminating rivers, fish, farm products, and drinking water. The symposium, titled “Addressing Mercury Pollution: Collaborative Solutions for Sustainable Mining in Ghana,” was organized by the U.S. Embassy on behalf of the Regional Environment, Science, Technology, and Health Hub for West and Central Africa to unite various sectors in reducing mercury use and promoting sustainable mining practices.

The environmental impact of mercury use in mining is documented through several specific findings. A 2024 baseline assessment by the US Geological Survey in Ghana's Western Region found that total mercury in unfiltered water from the Ankobra and Pra rivers was more than 55 times higher than the US average, while river sediments were two to 25 times higher. Additionally, turbidity—a measure of water cloudiness—in the Birim River reportedly reached 63 million Nephelometric Turbidity Units (NTU), significantly exceeding the maximum treatable level of 200 NTU and rendering a community water treatment plant unable to function. Sarah Cobb of the US Bureau of Oceans and International Environmental and Scientific Affairs (OES) noted that the scale of destruction is largely attributed to illegal small-scale mining and the indiscriminate use of mercury to extract gold.

Health experts highlighted that mercury pollution poses severe risks to human biology, including potential harm to developing brains, heart tissue, and reproductive health for pregnant mothers and their babies. To combat these issues, Sarah Cobb cited existing Ghanaian initiatives, such as a five-step anti-galamsey plan and a drone-equipped command centre operated by the Minerals Commission. The visit to the facilities included the Single Point Mooring (SPM), the oil jetty, and the Conventional Buoy Mooring (CBM). The CBM facility is located approximately 2.7 nautical miles from the Tema Fishing Harbour and uses four permanent mooring chains anchored to the seabed to keep vessels stationary and secured.

Kwadwo Opoku, Executive Director of the Institute for Energy Policy and Research, spoke on behalf of the visiting civil society groups and commended NPA Chief Executive Godwin Kudzo Tameklo for maintaining an open-door policy that provides stakeholders with deeper insight into operations within the downstream petroleum sector.

cards.headline: RCMP release photo of Moncton man charged with child luring and human trafficking

pages.text: Codiac Regional RCMP have released a photo of 45-year-old Timothy Roy, a former realtor in greater Moncton, New Brunswick, who faces several charges following a child luring investigation. Police also released a list of various communities across Canada where Roy has “spent time in” since 2000, including locations in Ontario, British Columbia, Nova Scotia, and Labrador. Investigators are encouraging anyone who may have had interactions with Roy or believes they may have been victimized to contact the RCMP or local police in their area.

The investigation began on Aug. 26 after police received information that a 45-year-old man was in contact with underage girls for a sexual purpose. On the evening of Sept. 10, officers located a vehicle belonging to the suspect parked at a hotel on Mountain Road in Moncton. The following day, the man was seen exiting the hotel with a female under the age of 16 and was arrested at the scene, according to RCMP spokesperson Cpl. Luc Picard. Roy was charged in Moncton provincial court on Sept. 15 and remains in custody pending a future court appearance. He faces charges of sexual assault, sexual interference of a person under the age of 16, human trafficking of a person under 18, child luring, and obtaining sexual services for consideration from a person under 18.

cards.headline: Approximately 200 unarmed police officers deployed to Nalerigu, Ghana, for NDC regional election

pages.text: About 200 unarmed police officers arrived at Nalerigu Senior High School on Saturday, November 14, 2026, to provide security for the National Democratic Congress (NDC) regional executive election. The police stated the deployment is intended to guarantee a free, fair, and orderly election involving a total of 231 delegates. While the officers on-site are unarmed, the police disclosed that armed personnel have been placed on standby to respond to any eventuality that might threaten security during the exercise. A commander urged candidates, supporters, and party stakeholders to conduct themselves responsibly to avoid undermining the electoral process.

The security presence follows deepening divisions within the NDC in the Nalerigu-Gambaga Constituency, which have led to legal disputes and public exchanges between rival party executives. These disagreements involve the selection and legitimacy of five co-opted constituency executives and whether they are eligible to participate in the regional election. Consequently, an application to the Nalerigu High Court resulted in a restraint preventing five individuals from participating in the election. Internal tensions have also surfaced a political rivalry between Regional Minister Ibrahim Tia and Alhaji Baba Issifu, a former Nalerigu-Gambaga MP and former Minister for Climate Change, regarding political influence in the constituency.

cards.headline: Village inside Karnataka's Bhadra Wildlife Sanctuary lacks roads, schools, and hospitals

pages.text: Residents of Paradeshappana Mutt, a village located near Sirivase in Chikkamagaluru taluk, live without roads, public transport, schools, hospitals, or electricity supply from utility companies. Situated deep inside the Bhadra Wildlife Sanctuary in Karnataka, the village is home to approximately 30 families. The majority of these residents belong to the Adi Karnataka, a Scheduled Caste, though a couple of residents do not. The village is named after a mutt that has existed there for centuries.

The lack of infrastructure forces residents to travel on foot or by personal two-wheeler to the nearest village, Bogase, even for basic essentials like salt. While houses have recently been lit at night using solar panels donated by private companies, Rudraiah, a resident in his 70s, and his cousin Kalaiah stated they had never seen a lightbulb in their homes before. Due to the absence of local schools, families send their children to stay with relatives or in hostels in distant locations for their studies.

cards.headline: Dozens of Afghans in US experience relief as deportation plans appear paused

pages.text: Dozens of Afghans currently in the United States are experiencing what Shawn VanDiver, founder and president of the non-profit coalition #AfghanEvac, described as “fragile relief” after it appeared the Trump administration put on hold plans to remove them within days. The group, which includes individuals who fear being killed by the Taliban if returned to Afghanistan, faced potential deportation following the expiration of a temporary court order that had previously blocked a flight scheduled for election day. The New York Times reported that the total group numbers more than 150 Afghans. The Associated Press previously reported that the federal government intends to route these detainees to their home country via Pakistan.

This development followed concerns from immigration advocates that detainees could have been forced to leave the US during the week of 16 November. cards.headline: Researchers find fossilized evidence of blood in 115-million-year-old dinosaur bone

pages.text: Researchers have discovered fossilized evidence of blood inside a 115-million-year-old dinosaur leg bone. A team led by Kliti Grice, a geochemist from Curtin University in Australia, found molecular evidence of heme—an iron-rich molecule found in blood—inside the bone. This discovery, published in the journal PNAS, includes the identification of microscopic structures that resemble red blood cells and other chemical fingerprints of blood. The findings suggest that certain biomolecules can persist much longer than previously thought when preserved under special burial conditions.

cards.headline: Archaeological discoveries in Saudi Arabia reveal human activity dating back around 125,000 years

pages.text: Archaeological discoveries at the Uruq Al-Julaybah site in Najran, Saudi Arabia, have revealed evidence of human activity dating back around 125,000 years. The findings, published in the journal Science, indicate that the area was once part of a lush environment featuring freshwater lakes and grasslands during a humid period of the Arabian Peninsula's history. This site was located on the shores of the Mundafan paleolake, a former body of water that researchers suggest covered approximately 340 square kilometers and reached depths of nearly 29 meters. These conditions provided a stable freshwater environment and abundant wildlife that supported early human settlement in what is now part of the Empty Quarter.

The multidisciplinary study was conducted by the Kingdom’s Heritage Commission in collaboration with King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST), Australia’s Griffith University, and several other Saudi and international research institutions. Researchers documented more than 130 archaeological locations and recorded more than 500 fossils of plants, vertebrates, and invertebrates. These fossils included hippopotamuses, extinct long-horned buffalo, camels, Arabian oryx, gazelles, ostriches, mollusks, and freshwater crustaceans. The team also recovered 5,511 stone artifacts, with more than 98 percent made from flint. Analysis showed these tools were created using the Levallois technique, an advanced stone-tool manufacturing method that requires precision and planning to control the specific shape and size of flakes and points.

Microscopic and chemical examinations of the artifacts identified preserved traces of wood, resins, fats, collagen, and plant fibers, suggesting daily activities involving both animal and plant resources. Some stone points showed evidence of hafting—the process of attaching a tool to a handle—as well as impact fractures. While researchers detected compounds from Acokanthera schimperi, a plant historically linked to hunting, the study noted there was insufficient evidence to determine exactly how the material was used. Abdullah Alsharekh of King Saud University stated the Mundafan shores provided an ideal habitat by combining freshwater, vegetation, and raw materials for survival. Professor Michael Petraglia of Griffith University said the discovery advances the understanding of early human settlement in the region, while KAUST geology professor Dr. Frans van Buchem noted the effort helped create a more complete picture of ancient human behavior.

cards.headline: Inactivating part of a patient's right amygdala reduced PTSD symptoms and threat perception

pages.text: A case study published in Nature Communications involving a man with drug-resistant epilepsy and severe post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) suggests that activity in the right amygdala may help sustain PTSD symptoms. During an awake bedside procedure, researchers selectively inactivated part of the man's right amygdala, which reduced his tendency to perceive ambiguous faces as fearful and was followed by a sharp drop in his trauma symptoms. While the findings are drawn from a single patient, they offer unusual causal evidence regarding how the amygdala contributes to threat-focused biases and PTSD symptoms. Standard brain imaging typically only captures correlations, leaving it uncertain whether abnormal amygdala activity drives negative interpretation bias or merely accompanies it. Studying targeted neurosurgery offers a rare way to observe the effects of directly disrupting amygdala function.

PTSD is a psychiatric condition that can develop after severe trauma, characterized by intrusive memories, avoidance of trauma reminders, negative shifts in mood and thinking, and persistent physical jumpiness. A central feature of the disorder is negative interpretation bias, which is the tendency to read neutral or ambiguous cues, such as an unreadable facial expression, as threatening. This bias can cause individuals to see everyday surroundings as dangerous, keeping fear responses active and making emotions harder to regulate. The amygdala—a pair of almond-shaped neuron clusters located deep inside the brain’s left and right temporal lobes, roughly behind the temples—helps detect danger and coordinate fear responses. Brain scans consistently show heightened amygdala reactivity to fearful or neutral sights in people with PTSD.

cards.headline: Forensic examination of 5,000-year-old skulls suggests human sacrifice in ancient Egypt

pages.text: A modern forensic examination of 46 skulls recovered near royal tombs in Abydos, Egypt, has uncovered signs of potentially deadly head trauma in 18 of the remains. This finding, representing approximately 39% of the individuals studied, provides new evidence suggesting that some of ancient Egypt's earliest rulers had members of their royal households killed upon their deaths, possibly to allow those individuals to continue serving them in the afterlife. The skulls belonged to members of the First Dynasty, who were buried roughly 5,000 years ago near the earliest kings of a unified Egypt. The research was led by Dr. Roselyn Campbell of Purdue University and published in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology.

The discovery provides physical evidence for a burial practice that archaeologists suspected more than a century ago but could not prove. When archaeologist Flinders Petrie excavated the graves in the 1920s, he observed that unusually large numbers of people were buried around the kings. While Petrie suspected these individuals had been sacrificed following the deaths of their rulers, he was unable to identify physical evidence of fatal injuries at that time. Dr. Campbell, who is also the author of the forthcoming book State-sanctioned Violence and Human Sacrifice in Early Dynastic Egypt (Routledge Press), noted that these retainers are often relegated to footnotes in the broader historical narrative and raised questions regarding how these individuals viewed the ruler and their own roles in the ruler's life and death.

cards.headline: Large Asian elephant herds in Sri Lanka fracture into smaller, less resilient groups after member losses

pages.text: Large herds of Asian elephants in Sri Lanka reach a tipping point where they fracture into smaller, isolated groups following losses from poaching, old age, disease, or drought. These smaller groups are more susceptible to further losses from the same external threats, reducing the overall resilience of the population. Unlike African elephants, which live in unrelated bachelor herds and related matriarch-led families, Asian elephant society is more fluid, with unrelated members frequently joining or leaving groups. In both species, offspring generally benefit from the protection and care provided by a larger number of adults. Researchers tracking 443 female elephants over 12 years initially identified 20 groups with an average of 14 members each.

The study, published in the journal Science, was led by University of California, San Diego Assistant Professor Shermin de Silva. Behavioral ecologist Anastasia Madsen, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Cincinnati, analyzed the data on wild elephants in Sri Lanka for the University of California, San Diego as part of a long-term demographic project. The research notes that elephants in Sri Lanka live in suboptimal habitats increasingly dominated by an inedible invasive species and live near human populations, leading to frequent deadly conflicts for both elephants and people.

cards.headline: Touch-based brain interface enables control of extra robotic arms during manual tasks

pages.text: Researchers have developed a touch-based brain-computer interface that allows people to command extra robotic arms while simultaneously using their own hands without disrupting natural physical coordination, according to a study published in Nature Communications by Jia et al. (2026). A brain-computer interface is a system that measures electrical activity in the brain, often through small sensors resting against the scalp, and translates specific signal patterns into commands for external machines. While much research in this field focuses on restoring movement for those with paralysis or injury, this work explores movement augmentation, which involves equipping able-bodied individuals with extra robotic limbs or fingers to perform tasks beyond the capacity of two biological hands. Tianyu Jia, a postdoctoral researcher in bioengineering at Imperial College London, noted that the initial inspiration for the project came partly from the fictional Spider-Man character Doctor Octopus.

In the study, volunteers used the interface to select among four distinct robotic commands. To do this, four small vibrators were strapped to the upper and lower arms, each buzzing in short bursts in a random order. Each vibrator represented a different command; by focusing attention on a specific vibration, participants triggered a brainwave response that the system decoded to move the robotic arms. To test if this could be done while multitasking, participants performed a manual ball-balancing task using a clear tray. After three days of practice, the accuracy gap between participants moving both their hands and those sitting still was no longer statistically significant.

cards.headline: Evolution may have altered instructions for producing brain-building cells

pages.text: Researchers in Taiwan and Japan have identified a small region of DNA that helps control the production of specialized neural stem cells, suggesting that evolution can create new developmental possibilities without necessarily creating entirely new genes. This finding, published in the journal Science Advances, provides a new perspective on how the primate brain achieves its size and complexity compared to other mammals. While previous discoveries showed how genetic changes can increase the number of brain cells or extend how long those cells multiply, this research indicates that evolution may also alter the instructions that determine which specific types of brain-building cells are produced.

The study was led by researchers at National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University (NYCU) and Academia Sinica, with collaborators from Kyoto University. To understand the mechanism, the researchers compared the process to a factory where neural stem cells act as workers that produce the cells making up the brain. In this model, evolution can change the brain by expanding the workforce, extending production hours, or changing the operating instructions to produce a different mix of workers. This discovery identifies the latter mechanism: a change in the instructions used to produce specific types of cells.

cards.headline: Yale scientists identify treatments that influence biological aging

pages.text: Scientists at Yale have identified that certain prescription medications and lifestyle changes can reduce biological age as measured by DNA-based blood tests, while popular over-the-counter supplements showed little evidence of producing similar effects. The findings, published in Nature Medicine, aim to help researchers more effectively evaluate anti-aging treatments by distinguishing between those that influence biological aging and those that show little measurable benefit. However, researchers emphasize that changes in biological age markers do not necessarily mean individuals will live longer or avoid age-related diseases.

The research was conducted by Raghav Sehgal, an associate research scientist in psychiatry at the Yale School of Medicine who specializes in computational biology and bioinformatics. Sehgal, who previously planned to use computer science techniques to investigate cancer, shifted his research focus toward the underlying aging process that contributes to the development of diseases such as cancer, diabetes, and dementia. He noted that researchers still have a long way to go in understanding the aging process and determining if management steps are truly effective.
